questions.problem:
Consider a function $q(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L{q(t)}=Q(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L{{e}^{9t}q(t)}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{9t}q(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,q(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{9t}q(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{9t}\,q(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-9)t}\,q(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $Q(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,q(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s-9)t}\,q(t)\,\text{d}t=Q(s-9),
$$

where 

$$
s-9>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}+9.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Graph Shifts From the First Shifting Theorem
questions.problem: Consider a function $f(t)$ for which the Laplace transform is $L{f(t)}=F(s).$ How can we obtain the graph of $L{{e}^{-9t}f(t)}$ from the graph of $F(s)?$
questions.worked_solution:
The first shifting theorem states that if
$L{f(t)}=F(s),$
then
$L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$

This implies that multiplying a function $f(t)$ by ${e}^{at}$ shifts the corresponding Laplace transform horizontally along the $s$-axis.

- If $a>0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the right.

- If $a<0,$ the graph of $F(s)$ shifts to the left.

In our case, to get the graph of $L{{e}^{-9t}f(t)},$ we must shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $9$ units to the left.

answer_fields.correct_value: Shift the graph of $F(s)$ by $9$ units to the left.

The first shifting theorem states that if

then

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the First Shifting Theorem and Linearity
questions.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t)=7{t}^{2}+5{t}^{4}{e}^{t}$ for $s>1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{7{t}^{2}+5{t}^{4}{e}^{t}} \\  & =L{7{t}^{2}}+L{5{t}^{4}{e}^{t}} \\  & =7L{{t}^{2}}+5L{{t}^{4}{e}^{t}}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{2}} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}} \\ L{{t}^{4}} & =\frac{24}{{s}^{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L{f(t)}=F(s),$ then $L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
L{{t}^{4}{e}^{t}}=\frac{24}{(s-1)^{5}}.
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =7L{{t}^{2}}+5L{{t}^{4}{e}^{t}} \\  & =7\cdot \frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+5\cdot \frac{24}{(s-1)^{5}} \\  & =\frac{14}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{120}{(s-1)^{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>1.$

questions.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of  $f(t)={e}^{-4t}+5{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}$ for $s>3.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{-4t}+5{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{-4t}}+L{5{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}} \\  & =L{{e}^{-4t}}+5L{{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}}\end{aligned}
$$

We are given that, for $s>0,$

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{n}} & =\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{2}} & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

The first shifting theorem states that if $L{f(t)}=F(s),$ then $L{{e}^{at}f(t)}=F(s-a).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}} & =\frac{2}{(s-3)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =L{{e}^{-4t}}+5L{{t}^{2}{e}^{3t}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+4}+5\cdot \frac{2}{(s-3)^{3}} \\  & =\frac{1}{s+4}+\frac{10}{(s-3)^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This transform is valid for $s>3.$
